newsitem.title: UK: Copper stock declines exacarbated by tight scrap.
newsitem.headline: Copper stock declines exacarbated by tight scrap.

text.p: Tightness of copper scrap supplies, both in Europe and North America, has compounded the long run of declines in warehouse stocks of primary metal - a situation likely to continue, traders said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) stocks of Grade A copper cathodes have fallen since the beginning of September from 275,775 tonnes to a six-year low of 132,350 tonnes this week.

There are several factors behind this sweeping drawdown, such as arbitrage shipments to the U.S. and China and reports of a general pick-up in consumption. But fabricators switching away from scrap towards cathode is another element in the equation.
"A lot of the brass mills are picking up standard cathodes or even Grade A, because their scrap stock has been priced at higher levels earlier this year," one trader said.
"So although there is scrap there, we won't see it until prices are higher," he said.
On the LME, cash copper prices have fallen from just over $2,800 in May to current levels of $2,000 a tonne in the shake-out following the Sumitomo Corp scandal.
Scrap prices, which follow LME values, have also dropped but at the same time the discount to the LME has been whittled away.
In the UK, number one bright wire copper scrap is currently quoted at 1,150/1,200 stg a tonne - just under the LME sterling equivalent for cash.
At the beginning of 1996 this scrap was at a 95-stg discount to the LME, having been as low as 150 stg under in August 1995.
Off-grade standard copper, which also runs at a discount to the LME, is now also virtually level, traders said.
"Because of the scrap tightness, some of the smaller foundrys are paying premiums of around 40 stg to get material," a scrap trader said.
However, most fabricators will probably continue to use primary metal for their intake, even though number one bright wire has a high copper content.
"It is all about margins at these price levels. Costs for melting losses are proportionally higher then when the market was firmer a year ago," the scrap trader said.
